🔑 MASTER FORMULA & KEY-FACTS SHEET (keep for revision)

Unit 1 (Relations & Functions):

  • A relation is a set of ordered pairs; domain = set of first coordinates, range = set of second coordinates.
  • Function: no two distinct ordered pairs share the same first element.
  • Vertical Line Test: a graph is a function iff no vertical line meets it more than once.
  • One-to-one (injective): each domain element has a distinct image. Onto (surjective): each co-domain element has a pre-image. Bijective = one-to-one AND onto.
  • Sum (f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x); Difference (f−g)(x)=f(x)−g(x); Product (fg)(x)=f(x)g(x); Quotient (f/g)(x)=f(x)/g(x), g(x)≠0.
  • Domain of combinations = intersection of domains (g≠0 for quotient).
  • Linear: f(x)=ax+b, a≠0; slope = a, y-intercept (0,b), x-intercept (−b/a, 0). a>0 increasing, a<0 decreasing, a=0 horizontal.
  • Quadratic: f(x)=ax²+bx+c, a≠0; vertex (−b/2a, (4ac−b²)/4a); axis x=−b/2a; opens up if a>0, down if a<0.
  • Completing the square: ax²+bx+c = a(x+b/2a)² + (4ac−b²)/4a.
  • Vertex form y=a(x−k)²+c → vertex (k,c).
  • Min/max value = c in vertex form; range {y≥c} if a>0, {y≤c} if a<0.
  • Sketching inequality regions: solid line for ≤/≥, broken line for </>.

Unit 2 (Polynomial Functions):

  • Polynomial: p(x)=aₙxⁿ+aₙ₋₁xⁿ⁻¹+…+a₀, n non-negative integer, aₙ≠0. Degree n, leading coefficient aₙ, constant term a₀.
  • Domain of any polynomial = ℝ.
  • Operations: sum/difference/product of polynomials are polynomials; degree of product = sum of degrees.
  • Polynomial Division Theorem: f(x)=d(x)q(x)+r(x), r=0 or deg r < deg d.
  • Remainder Theorem: remainder of f(x)÷(x−c) = f(c).
  • Factor Theorem: f(c)=0 ⟺ (x−c) is a factor of f(x).
  • Zero of f: value c with f(c)=0 (root of f(x)=0). Multiplicity k if (x−c)ᵏ is a factor but (x−c)ᵏ⁺¹ is not.
  • Location Theorem: if f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs, there's a zero between a and b.
  • Rational Zero Test: for p/q in lowest terms to be a zero, p divides a₀ and q divides aₙ.
  • Graph: smooth & continuous, no sharp corners; degree n has at most n−1 turning points, at most n x-intercepts.
  • Odd degree: ends opposite directions (LC>0: up right/down left; LC<0: down right/up left). Even degree: same direction both ends (LC>0 up; LC<0 down).

Unit 3 (Exponential & Logarithmic):

  • Laws of exponents: aᵐ·aⁿ=aᵐ⁺ⁿ; aᵐ/aⁿ=aᵐ⁻ⁿ; (aᵐ)ⁿ=aᵐⁿ; (ab)ⁿ=aⁿbⁿ; (a/b)ⁿ=aⁿ/bⁿ; a⁰=1 (a≠0); a⁻ⁿ=1/aⁿ.
  • Rational exponent: aᵐ/ⁿ=(a^1/n)^m; a^(1/n)=ⁿ√a.
  • Logarithm definition: logₐc = b ⟺ aᵇ = c (a>0, a≠1, c>0).
  • Properties: logₐ1=0; logₐa=1; logₐaᵖ=p; a^(logₐp)=p.
  • Laws: logₐ(MN)=logₐM+logₐN; logₐ(M/N)=logₐM−logₐN; logₐMʳ=r·logₐM.
  • Change of base: logₐM = log_b M / log_b a.
  • Common log = base 10 (written log M); natural log = base e (ln x). e≈2.718281828.
  • Exponential function f(x)=aˣ (a>0, a≠1): domain ℝ, range (0,∞), y-int (0,1), horizontal asymptote y=0. a>1 increasing, 0<a<1 decreasing.
  • Log function f(x)=logₐx: domain (0,∞), range ℝ, x-int (1,0), vertical asymptote x=0. a>1 increasing, 0<a<1 decreasing.
  • y=logₐx is the inverse (reflection in y=x) of y=aˣ.
  • Compound interest: A(t)=P(1+r/n)^(nt); continuously: A(t)=Pe^(rt).
  • Population growth: P(t)=P₀e^(kt). pH=−log[H⁺] (pH<7 acidic, =7 neutral, >7 basic).

Unit 4 (Trigonometric Functions):

  • π rad = 180°. Radian = degree × π/180; degree = radian × 180/π.
  • Arc length: l = rθ (θ in radians).
  • sinθ=y/r, cosθ=x/r, tanθ=y/x (for point P(x,y), r=√(x²+y²)).
  • cscθ=1/sinθ, secθ=1/cosθ, cotθ=1/tanθ.
  • sin²θ+cos²θ=1; 1+tan²θ=sec²θ; 1+cot²θ=csc²θ.
  • Reference angle θ_R: quadrant rules (QII: 180°−θ; QIII: θ−180°; QIV: 360°−θ).
  • Complementary: sinθ=cos(90°−θ); supplementary: sinθ=sin(180°−θ), cosθ=−cos(180°−θ).
  • Co-terminal: θ±360°n (or θ±2πn).
  • Addition: sin(α±β)=sinαcosβ±cosαsinβ; cos(α±β)=cosαcosβ∓sinαsinβ.
  • Double angle: sin2θ=2sinθcosθ; cos2θ=cos²θ−sin²θ=1−2sin²θ=2cos²θ−1; tan2θ=2tanθ/(1−tan²θ).
  • Half angle: sin(α/2)=±√((1−cosα)/2); cos(α/2)=±√((1+cosα)/2).
  • Sine & cosine: period 2π, range [−1,1], domain ℝ. Tangent: period π, domain {θ≠nπ/2, n odd}, range ℝ.
  • Sign table (sin,cos,tan): QI +,+,+; QII +,−,−; QIII −,−,+; QIV −,+,−.

Unit 5 (Circles):

  • Circle = locus of points equidistant from a center; A=πr², P=2πr.
  • Line of symmetry: any diameter; a circle has infinitely many.
  • Center-to-midpoint-of-chord is ⟂ to chord (Thm 5.1).
  • Perpendicular from center bisects the chord (Thm 5.2).
  • Equal chords are equidistant from center (Thm 5.3); equal chords subtend equal central angles (Thm 5.5).
  • Inscribed angle = ½ central angle intercepting same arc (Thm 5.6).
  • Inscribed angles subtending same arc are equal (Thm 5.7).
  • Angle in a semicircle is a right angle (Thales, Thm 5.8).
  • Cyclic quadrilateral: opposite angles sum to 180° (Thm 5.9).
  • Arc length: s=2πr·θ/360°. Chord length: l=2r·sin(θ/2).
  • Area of sector = πr²·θ/360°. Perimeter of sector = 2r + arc.
  • Area of segment = sector − triangle = πr²θ/360 − ½r²sinθ.
  • Intersecting chords inside: angle = ½(sum of intercepted arcs) (Thm 5.10).
  • Secants/tangents outside: angle = ½(difference of intercepted arcs) (Thm 5.11).

Unit 6 (Solid Figures):

  • Prism: LSA=ph; TSA=LSA+2BA; V=BA·h.
  • Cylinder: LSA=2πrh; TSA=2πr(h+r); V=πr²h.
  • Regular pyramid: LSA=½pl (p=perimeter, l=slant height); TSA=BA+½pl; V=⅓(BA)h.
  • Cone: LSA=πrl; TSA=πr(l+r); V=⅓πr²h. l=√(h²+r²).
  • Sphere: SA=4πr²; V=4/3πr³.
  • Horizontal cross-section of pyramid/cone: ratio of area = k²/h² (k=dist from vertex).
  • Frustum of pyramid: LSA=½l(p+p′); V=⅓h(A+A′+√(AA′)).
  • Frustum of cone: LSA=πl(r+r′); TSA=πl(r+r′)+π(r²+r′²); V=⅓πh(r²+r′²+rr′).
  • Composed solids: total volume = sum of parts; surface area = sum of exposed surfaces.

Unit 7 (Coordinate Geometry):

  • Distance: d=√((x₂−x₁)²+(y₂−y₁)²).
  • Section formula (internal p:q): R=((p x₂+q x₁)/(p+q), (p y₂+q y₁)/(p+q)).
  • Midpoint: M=((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2).
  • Slope/gradient: m=(y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁), x₁≠x₂; m=tanθ (θ = inclination).
  • Point-slope: y−y₁=m(x−x₁). Slope-intercept: y=mx+b.
  • Two-point form: y−y₁=((y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁))(x−x₁). General: Ax+By+C=0.
  • Parallel lines: m₁=m₂. Perpendicular: m₁·m₂=−1.
  • Circle (standard): (x−h)²+(y−k)²=r²; center origin: x²+y²=r².
  • Circle (general): x²+y²+lx+my+n=0, l²+m²−4n>0.
  • Area of triangle: A=½|x₁(y₂−y₃)+x₂(y₃−y₁)+x₃(y₁−y₂)|.

🎯 TOP 15 EXAM TRAPS (quick scan)

  1. a≠0 for quadratic/linear — f(x)=ax²+bx+c with a=0 is not quadratic.
  2. Domain of f/g excludes g=0 and intersection of domains.
  3. Remainder Theorem needs divisor of form (x−c) — for (ax+b) remainder is f(−b/a).
  4. Zero vs factor direction — f(c)=0 ⟺ (x−c) factor (both directions).
  5. Polynomial exponents must be non-negative integers — 1/x, √x, x⁻² are NOT polynomials.
  6. logₐx requires x>0 — state the universe before solving log equations.
  7. log(MN)≠logM·logN and log(M+N)≠logM+logN — no product/sum inside log.
  8. Exponential base a≠1 — 1ˣ is constant, not exponential.
  9. Sine/cosine range is [−1,1] — never ≥1 in magnitude.
  10. Tangent undefined at odd multiples of π/2 — vertical asymptotes.
  11. Angle in a semicircle is 90° — not the central angle.
  12. Inscribed angle = HALF the central angle, not equal.
  13. Segment area = sector − triangle, subtract the triangle!
  14. Frustum volume = ⅓h(A+A′+√(AA′)) — the √(AA′) term is easy to forget.
  15. Perpendicular slopes multiply to −1 (reciprocal + opposite sign), not just negative.

UNIT 1: RELATIONS AND FUNCTIONS

Note: Based on the official ANRSEB Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook (new curriculum, 2023), Unit 1.

1.1 Relations

A relation is a set of ordered pairs. In daily life we meet relations such as "m is greater than n," "line n is perpendicular to line m," brothers/sisters, teachers/students. In mathematics a relation links two things by a relating phrase (e.g., y = 2x, y > x, y ≤ x+2, x²+y²=1).

  • The set of first components of the ordered pairs is the domain of the relation.
  • The set of second components is the range of the relation.

Example: If R = {(x,y): y = 2x} where x,y are integers, then R contains (−2,−4),(−1,−2),(0,0),(1,2),(2,4). Domain = all integers; Range = all even integers.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: A relation is just a set of ordered pairs. Domain = set of first coordinates; Range = set of second coordinates. To find them, list what x-values and y-values actually occur.

1.1.4 Graphs of Relations

We can represent a relation graphically by plotting its ordered pairs in a Cartesian (xy) coordinate system.

To sketch the graph of a relation given by an inequality:

  1. Draw the graph of the boundary line(s).
  2. Use a solid line if the inequality is ≤ or ≥; use a broken (dashed) line if it is < or >.
  3. Take arbitrary test points on each side of the line.
  4. The region containing points that satisfy the relation is the graph.

Example (y > x): Draw y=x as a dashed line (points on it NOT included). Test (0,3) → 3>0 true, and (0,−2) → false. So the solution region is above the line y=x.

Graph of the relation y > x

Example (y ≤ x+2): Draw y=x+2 as a solid line. Test (1,0): 0≤1+2 true. Shade the region below the line containing (1,0).

Graph of the relation y ≤ x+2
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Solid line for ≤/≥ (boundary included), broken/dashed line for </> (boundary excluded). Always test a point not on the line to decide which side to shade.

Systems of inequalities: The graph of a system such as {y<x AND y>−x+2} is the overlap of the two individual regions. Solve the boundary equations to find the intersection point.

Graph of a system of two inequalities

Example: For {y<x and y>−x+2}, the intersection of the two lines is x=1 (from x = −x+2). Test (2,0): 2<0 is false, but in the worked example (2,0) satisfied both — check signs carefully. Domain = {x : x>1}, Range = ℝ.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: The graph of a relation given by an inequality is a region, not a curve. The graph of a relation given by an equation is a curve.

1.2 Functions

1.2.1 The notion of function

Definition (Function): A function f is a set of ordered pairs with the property that whenever (x,y) and (x,z) belong to f, then y=z. Equivalently: a relation in which no two distinct ordered pairs have the same first element.

  • Repeated first elements are allowed only if they map to the same second element. Example: {(1,5),(1,5),(3,−8),(3,−8),(7,4)} IS a function (duplicates removed).
  • R={(2,3),(5,3),(3,6),(7,6),(5,8)} is NOT a function because (5,3) and (5,8) share first element 5 but differ.

Domain, co-domain, range:

  • Domain = set of all input (x) values.
  • Co-domain = set of all possible outputs (B in f:A→B).
  • Range = set of actual outputs f(x) (a subset of the co-domain).

Notation: f(x) is the image of x; x is the pre-image of f(x). f:A→B means domain is A and range ⊆ B.

Examples:

  • f(x)=3x+4: domain ℝ, range ℝ (every real has a pre-image).
  • f(x)=√(x−2): domain {x≥2}, range {y≥0}.
  • f(x)=1−3x²: domain ℝ; f(2)=1−12=−11, f(−1)=1−3=−2.
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: To find a domain: (i) denominators ≠ 0, (ii) expressions under even radicals ≥ 0. Evaluating f at a means substituting x=a into the formula.

1.2.2 Combination of functions

For two functions f and g with overlapping (intersecting) domains:

  • Sum: (f+g)(x) = f(x) + g(x)
  • Difference: (f−g)(x) = f(x) − g(x)
  • Product: (fg)(x) = f(x)·g(x)
  • Quotient: (f/g)(x) = f(x)/g(x), g(x)≠0

The domain of a combination = intersection of the domains of f and g; for the quotient, additionally exclude where g(x)=0.

Example: f(x)=x−5, g(x)=2x+1 → domain of f+g and f−g is ℝ (both domains are ℝ).

Example: f(x)=√x, g(x)=√(4−x²). Domain f=[0,∞), domain g=[−2,2]. Intersection = [0,2]. (f/g): g≠0 → [0,2). (g/f): f≠0 → (0,2].

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Domain of f/g = (domain f ∩ domain g) minus points where g(x)=0. Domain of fg = domain f ∩ domain g.

Vertical Line Test

A graph is the graph of a function if and only if no vertical line intersects the graph in more than one point. If a vertical line cuts a curve twice, the curve is NOT a function.

1.2.3 Types of functions

  • One-to-one (injective): each element of the domain has a distinct image. f:ℝ→ℝ, f(x)=3x+5 is one-to-one because f(x₁)=f(x₂) ⟹ 3x₁+5=3x₂+5 ⟹ x₁=x₂.
  • Onto (surjective): each element of the co-domain has at least one pre-image.
  • One-to-one correspondence (bijective): both injective and surjective.

Examples (fig. 1.19): (a) onto but not one-to-one; (b) both one-to-one and onto (bijective); (c) injective but not surjective; (d) neither injective nor surjective.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Injective ⟺ distinct x give distinct y. Surjective ⟺ range = co-domain. Bijective = injective + surjective. f(x)=x² on ℝ→ℝ is neither injective nor surjective.

1.2.4 Graphs of functions

Graph of a function = set of all points {(x, f(x)) : x ∈ domain}.

Linear function: f(x)=ax+b, a≠0. Constant function: f(x)=b.

  • Graph is a straight line.
  • a>0 → increasing; a<0 → decreasing; a=0 → horizontal.
  • Slope = a, y-intercept (0,b), x-intercept (−b/a, 0).
Linear functions with different slopes through (0,2)
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: In f(x)=ax+b, the coefficient a is the slope (steepness), b is the y-intercept. Bigger |a| → steeper line.

Quadratic function: f(x)=ax²+bx+c, a≠0. Graph is a parabola (U-shape).

  • If a>0 the parabola opens upward (has a minimum); if a<0 it opens downward (has a maximum).
  • Vertex (turning point): (−b/2a, (4ac−b²)/4a).
  • Axis of symmetry: the vertical line x=−b/2a through the vertex.
  • Domain = ℝ. Range = {y ≥ vertex-value} if a>0, {y ≤ vertex-value} if a<0.

Graphs of y=ax²: larger |a| makes the parabola narrower (steeper); smaller |a| wider.

The parabola family y=ax²

Graph of y=(x−k)²+c: shift y=x² right by k and up by c; vertex at (k,c).

Shifting y=x² to y=(x−3)²+2

Completing the square turns ax²+bx+c into vertex form:

ax²+bx+c = a(x + b/2a)² + (4ac−b²)/4a

so the vertex is (−b/2a, (4ac−b²)/4a).

Parabola y=x²+6x+11 = (x+3)²+2

Example: y=x²+6x+11 = (x+3)²+2 → vertex (−3,2), axis x=−3, y-intercept (0,11), no x-intercept (opens up, vertex above axis).

Example: y=−x²+2x+3 = −(x−1)²+4 → vertex (1,4), opens down, x-intercepts from −(x−1)²+4=0 → x=−1 or 3, y-intercept (0,3).

Parabola y=−x²+2x+3 (maximum)
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Vertex form y=a(x−k)²+c: vertex (k,c); minimum value c if a>0, maximum value c if a<0. Use completing the square to find the vertex of any quadratic.

1.3 Applications of Relations and Functions

Linear model (forensics): height = 2.47·(femur length) + 54, for 40≤length≤55. Femur 44 cm → height ≈ 2.47(44)+54 = 162.68 ≈ 163 cm. Femur 51 cm → ≈180 cm.

Maximum/minimum problems: A parabola reaches a max or min at its vertex. The minimum of f(x)=(x+k)²+c is c; the maximum of f(x)=−(x+k)²+c is c.

Maximum value example y=−(x−3)²+1

Example: f(x)=−x²+6x−8 = −(x−3)²+1 → vertex (3,1), maximum value 1, range {y≤1}=(−∞,1].

Graphical method of solving quadratic equations

  1. Rearrange so one side is zero.
  2. Draw the graph of the quadratic function.
  3. The x-coordinates where the curve crosses the x-axis are the solutions.
  • Crosses at two points → two real solutions.
  • Touches at one point → one (repeated) solution.
  • Never crosses → no real solutions.
Solving x²−4=0 graphically

Example: y=x²−4 crosses x-axis at x=−2 and x=2 → solutions of x²−4=0 are −2, 2.

Example: y=x²−2x−3=(x−1)²−4 has vertex (1,−4), crosses at x=−1 and x=3.

Example: y=x²+4x+8=(x+2)²+4 opens up, vertex (−2,4) above axis → no real solution.

Graphical method of solving quadratic inequalities

  1. Write in standard form ax²+bx+c≥0 or ≤0.
  2. Graph the parabola.
  3. ax²+bx+c<0 → the portion where the parabola is below the x-axis; >0 → above.
Quadratic inequality x²−6x+8<0

Example: x²−6x+8<0. Roots at x=2 and x=4; parabola opens up, so it is below the axis between the roots. Solution (2,4) i.e. {x: 2<x<4}.

Example: −x²−8x−12≤0 = −(x+4)²+4 ≤0. Roots −6 and −2; opens down, so ≤0 outside the roots. Solution (−∞,−6]∪[−2,∞).

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: For an upward parabola, <0 is between the roots, >0 is outside. For a downward parabola, <0 is outside the roots, >0 is between. Include endpoints only for ≤/≥.

📌 QUICK REVISION / MUST-KNOW BOX (Unit 1)

  • Relation = set of ordered pairs; domain = first coordinates, range = second.
  • Function: no two ordered pairs share the same first element (Vertical Line Test).
  • One-to-one (injective), onto (surjective), bijective (both).
  • Combinations: (f+g),(f−g),(fg),(f/g) with g≠0; domain = intersection of domains.
  • Linear f(x)=ax+b: slope a, y-int b, x-int −b/a; a>0 inc, a<0 dec.
  • Quadratic f(x)=ax²+bx+c: vertex (−b/2a,(4ac−b²)/4a), axis x=−b/2a; a>0 min/up, a<0 max/down.
  • Completing the square → vertex form y=a(x−k)²+c, vertex (k,c).
  • Inequality regions: solid for ≤/≥, dashed for </>; test a point to shade.
  • Quadratic equation solved graphically: read x-intercepts.
  • Quadratic inequality: solve by reading where parabola is above/below axis.

UNIT 2: POLYNOMIAL FUNCTIONS

Note: Based on the official ANRSEB Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook (new curriculum, 2023), Unit 2.

2.1 Definition of Polynomial Function

Definition (Polynomial function): Let n be a non-negative integer and let aₙ,aₙ₋₁,…,a₀ be real numbers with aₙ≠0. The function

p(x) = aₙxⁿ + aₙ₋₁xⁿ⁻¹ + … + a₂x² + a₁x + a₀

is called a polynomial function in one variable x of degree n.

Terminology:

  • Coefficients: aₙ,…,a₀.
  • Leading coefficient: aₙ (the nonzero coefficient of the highest power).
  • Leading term: aₙxⁿ.
  • Degree: n (the highest exponent).
  • Constant term: a₀.

Domain of any polynomial function = ℝ (all real numbers).

Examples:

  • f(x)=3x²+x−3: degree 2, leading coeff 3, constant −3.
  • g(x)=4x⁵−x⁴+3x³+(2/5)x²+5x−2: degree 5, leading coeff 4, constant −2.
  • g(x)=2(x⁴+½x²−2)+x+x⁴+1 = 3x⁴+x²+x−3: degree 4, leading coeff 3, constant −3.

Constant & zero polynomial:

  • f(x)=b, b≠0 → polynomial of degree 0.
  • f(x)=0 → the zero polynomial, no degree assigned.
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: A polynomial's exponents must be non-negative integers. Terms like x⁻², 1/x, √x, x^(1/2), x^(1/3) make a function NOT a polynomial. Also its domain must be all real numbers.

Non-polynomials: g(x)=4x⁻²+3x⁻¹−7 (negative exponents), h(x)=2ˣ (variable in exponent), k(y)=√y (radical), f(x)=2x^(1/3)+5x^(1/2)−x+5 (fractional exponents).

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: A polynomial function is over integers/rationals/reals if all its coefficients are integers/rationals/reals.

2.2 Operations on Polynomial Functions

Addition & Subtraction: add/subtract coefficients of like terms (same power of x). Remove brackets for subtraction.

  • (f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x); (f−g)(x)=f(x)−g(x).
  • Sum/difference of polynomials is a polynomial.
  • If degrees differ, degree of sum/diff = the larger degree; if same degree, the result may drop a degree (like terms cancel).

Multiplication: multiply each term of one by every term of the other (distributive property).

  • (fg)(x)=f(x)g(x).
  • If deg f = m and deg g = n (nonzero), then deg(fg) = m+n.
  • Product of polynomials is a polynomial; if either is the zero polynomial, the product is zero with no degree.

Division (long division): (f÷g)(x)=f(x)÷g(x), g(x)≠0.

  • Stop when the remainder has degree less than the divisor's degree.
  • Result written as f(x)/g(x) = q(x) + r(x)/g(x).
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Degree(fg) = degree f + degree g. Degree(f+g) = larger degree (or possibly lower if like terms cancel).

2.3 Theorems on Polynomials

Polynomial Division Theorem (Thm 2.1)

If f(x) and d(x) are polynomials with d(x)≠0 and deg d ≤ deg f, then there exist unique polynomials q(x) and r(x) such that

f(x) = d(x)q(x) + r(x)

where r(x)=0 or deg r < deg d. If r(x)=0, d(x) divides f(x) exactly.

Remainder Theorem (Thm 2.2)

Let f(x) be a polynomial of degree ≥1 and c any real number. If f(x) is divided by (x−c), the remainder is f(c).

  • The value of f at c equals the remainder when dividing by x−c.
  • Proof: f(x)=(x−c)q(x)+k, substitute x=c → f(c)=k.

Example: f(x)=x³−3x²+4, divide by x−1 → remainder f(1)=1−3+4=2.

Example: f(x)=2x³+5x²+3x+2, divide by x+1 (=x−(−1)) → c=−1 → remainder f(−1)=−2+5−3+2=2.

Example: 3x³−4x²+bx−5 divided by x−2 has remainder 10 → f(2)=24−16+2b−5=3+2b=10 → b=7/2... (check: the textbook gives b=7). Always set f(c)=given remainder and solve for the unknown.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: For divisor (ax+b), write it as a(x−(−b/a)); the remainder is f(−b/a).

Factor Theorem (Thm 2.3)

Let f(x) be a polynomial of degree ≥1 and c any real number. Then:

  1. If f(c)=0, then (x−c) is a factor of f(x).
  2. If (x−c) is a factor of f(x), then f(c)=0.

Example: x+2 is a factor of x²+5x+6 because f(−2)=(−2)²+5(−2)+6=0.

Example: f(x)=x⁴−x³−x²−x−2: f(−1)=0 (x+1 factor), f(2)=0 (x−2 factor), but f(−2)=20≠0 (x+2 not a factor).

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Factor theorem is the reverse of remainder theorem: remainder 0 ⟺ (x−c) is a factor.

2.4 Zeros of a Polynomial Function

Definition (Zero): For a polynomial f(x), a real number c is a zero if f(c)=0. (Zeros = roots of f(x)=0 = x-intercepts of the graph.)

  • If (x−c) is a factor, c is a zero (and vice versa).
  • To find zeros: set f(x)=0 and factor.

Example: f(x)=(x−2)(3x+4)(1−4x) → zeros x=2, x=−4/3, x=1/4.

Example: f(x)=x⁴−13x²+36=(x²−4)(x²−9)=(x−2)(x+2)(x−3)(x+3) → zeros ±2, ±3.

Multiplicity (Def 2.8)

If (x−c)ᵏ is a factor of f(x) but (x−c)ᵏ⁺¹ is not, then c is a zero of multiplicity k.

  • k=1 → simple zero. k>1 → repeated (multiple) zero.

Example: f(x)=x³+2x²−x−2=(x−1)(x+1)(x+2): all simple zeros.

g(x)=x³+4x²−3x−18=(x+3)²(x−2): zero −3 has multiplicity 2; zero 2 is simple.

Building a polynomial from zeros: If zeros are z₁,z₂,… and you need f(p)=k, use f(x)=a(x−z₁)(x−z₂)…, solve for a. Example: degree 2 with zeros 1,−2 and f(3)=30 → f(x)=a(x−1)(x+2); f(3)=a(2)(5)=10a=30 → a=3 → f(x)=3(x−1)(x+2).

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Zero of multiplicity m: if m is odd the graph crosses the x-axis; if m is even the graph touches (bounces off) the axis.

Location Theorem (Thm 2.4)

If f is a polynomial and f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs (a<b), then there is at least one zero of f between a and b.

Example: f(x)=x⁶−2x⁵−4x²+4x+4: f(1)=3>0, f(2)=−4<0 → zero between 1 and 2.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Opposite signs at two points guarantee a zero between them. Same signs give no guarantee.

Rational Zero Test (Thm 2.5)

If all coefficients of f(x)=aₙxⁿ+…+a₀ are integers (aₙ≠0, a₀≠0) and p/q in lowest terms is a zero, then p is a factor of a₀ and q is a factor of aₙ.

Steps: list factors of a₀ (p's), factors of aₙ (q's), form all ±p/q, test which give f(p/q)=0.

Example: f(x)=x²+x−2: p=±1,±2; q=±1; candidates ±1,±2. f(−2)=0, f(1)=0 → zeros −2, 1.

Example: f(x)=6x³+13x²+x−2: p=±1,±2; q=1,2,3,6 → candidates ±1,±½,±⅓,±⅙,±2,±⅔. f(−½)=f(−2)=f(⅓)=0 → zeros −½,−2,⅓ → factor f(x)=(3x−1)(2x+1)(x+2).

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Rational zeros are of the form (factor of constant term)/(factor of leading coefficient). This only finds RATIONAL zeros; irrational and complex zeros are missed.

2.5 Graphs of Polynomial Functions

Key properties (from observations):

  • Graph of a polynomial is smooth (no sharp corners) and continuous (no holes or jumps).
  • f(x)=|x| is NOT a polynomial (sharp corner at (0,0)); a graph with a hole/jump is not a polynomial.
Absolute value is not a polynomial (sharp corner)
  • A polynomial of degree n has at most n−1 turning points and intersects the x-axis at most n times.

Quadratic graph (degree 2):

Turning point of y=x²+2x−3

Odd degree (1,3,5,…): ends go in opposite directions.

  • Leading coefficient positive: up to the right, down to the left.
  • Leading coefficient negative: down to the right, up to the left.

Even degree (2,4,…): ends go in the same direction.

  • Leading coefficient positive: both ends up.
  • Leading coefficient negative: both ends down.
Cubic graphs y=x³−1 and y=−x³+1
Cubic end behaviour y=x³ and y=−x³
Quartic even-degree graphs

Example: f(x)=x³−1=(x−1)(x²+x+1): x-intercept 1, y-intercept −1, up right/down left (LC>0, odd).

f(x)=−x³+1: x-intercept 1, y-intercept 1, down right/up left.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Determine end behaviour from the degree (odd/even) and the sign of the leading coefficient. Find x-intercepts via factorization/rational zero test; use the location theorem to find where zeros sit.
Cubic with three x-intercepts

2.6 Applications

Maximum area problems (quadratic):

Example: A 56 m wire is bent into a rectangle. Perimeter 2x+2y=56 → y=28−x. Area A=x(28−x)=−x²+28x = 196−(x−14)². Maximum area 196 m² at x=14, y=14 (a square of side 14 m).

Example (min product): Two numbers differ by 16, minimize the product. y=x−16, A=x(x−16)=(x−8)²−64. Minimum product −64 at x=8, y=−8.

Open box (volume): Removing x×x squares from an 80×50 cm card gives V=4x³−260x²+4000x. (x=20 → compute; x cannot be 30 because two corners' squares would overlap: 2x≤50.)

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: In optimization word problems: (1) define variables, (2) write the quantity to optimize as a function, (3) put into vertex form by completing the square, (4) read the max/min and the x that gives it.

📌 QUICK REVISION / MUST-KNOW BOX (Unit 2)

  • Polynomial: exponents are non-negative integers; degree, leading coeff, constant term.
  • Domain of any polynomial = ℝ.
  • deg(fg)=deg f + deg g; sum/diff/product of polynomials are polynomials.
  • Polynomial Division: f=dq+r, r=0 or deg r<deg d.
  • Remainder Theorem: remainder of f÷(x−c) = f(c).
  • Factor Theorem: f(c)=0 ⟺ (x−c) factor.
  • Zero = root = x-intercept. Multiplicity k.
  • Location Theorem: sign change between a,b → zero between them.
  • Rational Zero Test: zeros = ±(factors of a₀)/(factors of aₙ).
  • Graph: smooth & continuous; degree n → at most n−1 turning points, at most n x-intercepts.
  • End behaviour: odd degree → ends opposite; even → same. Sign of leading coeff sets up/down.

UNIT 3: EXPONENTIAL AND LOGARITHMIC FUNCTIONS

Note: Based on the official ANRSEB Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook (new curriculum, 2023), Unit 3.

3.1 Exponents and Logarithms

3.1.1 Exponents

aⁿ means a multiplied by itself n times (n factors). a is the base, n is the exponent.

  • (−a)ⁿ: the base is −a. But −aⁿ: the base is only a. So (−3)²=9 but −3²=−9. (3a)³=27a³ but 3a³=3a³.

Laws of exponents (integer/rational/irrational exponents):

  1. aᵐ·aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ
  2. aᵐ/aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ (a≠0)
  3. (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ
  4. (ab)ⁿ = aⁿbⁿ
  5. (a/b)ⁿ = aⁿ/bⁿ (b≠0)

Zero & negative exponents (Def 3.2): a⁰=1 (a≠0); a⁻ⁿ=1/aⁿ. 0⁰ is undefined.

Rational exponents (Def 3.3, 3.4):

  • a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a (the nth root). For even n and negative a, it's undefined in reals; for odd n and negative a, it's defined (negative root).
  • a^(m/n) = (a^(1/n))ᵐ = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ.
  • a^(−m/n) = 1/(a^(m/n)).
  • Definition 3.5: a^(m/n) = ᵐ√(aᵐ) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ.

Irrational exponents: aᵇ (b irrational) is the real number that aˣ approaches as x→b (e.g., 3^√2 ≈ 4.7288). All the exponent laws hold for irrational exponents too.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: (−a)ⁿ vs −aⁿ differ by where the minus sign sits. a⁰=1 for a≠0. a⁻ⁿ=1/aⁿ.

3.1.2 Logarithms

Definition (Def 3.6): For a>0, a≠1, c>0: logₐc = b ⟺ aᵇ = c.

  • "logₐc" is the exponent to which a must be raised to get c.
  • log₂8=3 (2³=8); log₃(1/9)=−2 (3⁻²=1/9); log₅1=0 (5⁰=1).

Properties of logarithms:

  1. logₐ1 = 0
  2. logₐa = 1
  3. logₐaᵖ = p and a^(logₐp) = p (inverse property)
  4. If logₐM=logₐN then M=N (one-to-one property)

Laws of logarithms (M,N>0, a>0,a≠1):

  1. Product: logₐ(MN) = logₐM + logₐN
  2. Power: logₐ(Mʳ) = r·logₐM
  3. Quotient: logₐ(M/N) = logₐM − logₐN
  4. Change of base: logₐM = (log_b M)/(log_b a)

Common mistakes to avoid:

  • logₐ(MN) ≠ (logₐM)(logₐN)
  • logₐ(M+N) ≠ logₐM + logₐN
  • logₐ(M/N) ≠ (logₐM)/(logₐN)
  • (logₐM)ʳ ≠ r·logₐM
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: A logarithm is an exponent. Product→sum, quotient→difference, power→multiple. Never split log of a sum/product incorrectly.

Common logarithms (base 10): written log M (base 10 omitted). If p=m×10^c with 1≤m<10, then log p = log m + c, where log m is the mantissa and c is the characteristic.

Example: log 6,920 = log(6.92×10³) = log 6.92 + 3 = 0.8401 + 3 = 3.8401.

log 0.00123 = log(1.23×10⁻³) = 0.0899 + (−3) → characteristic −3, mantissa 0.0899.

Antilogarithm: If log M = N, then M = antilog(N). Use the antilog table; for a characteristic c, multiply by 10^c.

  • antilog(3.0913) = antilog(0.0913)×10³ = 1.234×1000 = 1234.
  • For negative: antilog(−2.1202): rewrite −2.1202 = −3 + 0.8798, then antilog(0.8798)×10⁻³ = 7.582×10⁻³ = 0.007582.

Computation with logarithms: To compute a number M: (1) find log M using the laws, (2) take the antilog.

Example: √254 → log = ½log254 = ½(2+log2.54)=1+½(0.4048)=1.2024 → antilog ≈ 15.93.

3.2 The Exponential Functions and Their Graphs

3.2.1 Exponential Functions

Definition (Def 3.8): The exponential function with base a is f(x)=aˣ where a>0, a≠1, and x is any real number.

  • a≠1 because 1ˣ=1 is constant.
  • The variable is in the exponent (unlike polynomials).

3.2.2 Graph of Exponential Functions

f(x)=2ˣ: domain ℝ, range (0,∞), y-intercept (0,1), no x-intercept, increasing, horizontal asymptote y=0 (x-axis).

Graph of f(x)=2ˣ

f(x)=(½)ˣ: domain ℝ, range (0,∞), y-int (0,1), decreasing, horizontal asymptote y=0.

Graph of f(x)=(½)ˣ

General shapes of y=aˣ:

  • a>1: increasing (rapid growth to the right, approaches x-axis to the left).
  • 0<a<1: decreasing (approaches x-axis to the right, rapid growth to the left).
Both exponential shapes y=3ˣ and y=(⅓)ˣ

Characteristics of y=aˣ (a>0,a≠1):

  • Domain ℝ; range ℝ⁺ (positive reals).
  • y-intercept (0,1); NO x-intercept.
  • Horizontal asymptote: the x-axis (y=0).
  • a>1 increasing; 0<a<1 decreasing.
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Exponential graph always passes through (0,1), never touches the x-axis, has y=0 as a horizontal asymptote. Increasing if a>1, decreasing if 0<a<1.

Natural exponential function (Def 3.9): f(x)=eˣ with base e ≈ 2.718281828… (e = limit of (1+1/n)ⁿ as n→∞). Since 2<e<3, its graph lies between 2ˣ and 3ˣ.

Natural exponential eˣ between 2ˣ and 3ˣ

Example: y=−eˣ has y-int (0,−1), no x-intercept, asymptote y=0, domain ℝ, range (negative reals), decreasing.

Graph of y=−eˣ

3.3 The Logarithmic Functions and Their Graphs

3.3.1 The Logarithmic Function

The inverse of y=aˣ (a>0,a≠1) is the logarithmic function g(x)=logₐx, defined by:

y = logₐx ⟺ x = aʸ.

Since aˣ has domain ℝ and range (0,∞), logₐx has domain (0,∞) and range ℝ.

Evaluating: log₂4=2 (2²=4); log₄1=0; log₃27=3; log₁₀(1/10)=−1.

3.3.2 Graphs of Logarithmic Functions

f(x)=log₂x: domain (0,∞), range ℝ, x-intercept (1,0), vertical asymptote x=0 (y-axis), increasing.

Graph of f(x)=log₂x

f(x)=log(½)x: domain (0,∞), range ℝ, x-int (1,0), vertical asymptote x=0, decreasing.

Graph of f(x)=log(½)x

General shapes of y=logₐx:

  • a>1: increasing.
  • 0<a<1: decreasing.
  • Both: x-intercept (1,0), vertical asymptote x=0.
Both logarithmic shapes

Characteristics of y=logₐx (a>0,a≠1):

  • Domain ℝ⁺ (positive reals); range ℝ.
  • x-intercept (1,0); NO y-intercept.
  • Vertical asymptote: the y-axis (x=0).
  • a>1 increasing; 0<a<1 decreasing.

Reflections:

  • Graph of −f(x) = reflection of f in the x-axis.
  • Graph of f(−x) = reflection of f in the y-axis.
Reflections of y=log₂x
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: logₐx passes through (1,0), never touches the y-axis (x=0 is a vertical asymptote), is increasing for a>1 and decreasing for 0<a<1.

3.3.3 Natural Logarithms

Definition (Def 3.10): log_e x = ln x (logarithm to base e).

  • ln 1=0; ln e=1; ln e³=3; ln(e^(1/3))=⅓; ln(1/e)=−1.
  • The graphs of y=eˣ and y=ln x are reflections of each other across the line y=x.
Graphs of y=eˣ, y=x, y=ln x (inverse pair)

3.4 Solving Exponential and Logarithmic Equations

3.4.1 Solving Exponential Equations

An exponential equation has the variable in the exponent (e.g., 2ˣ=16, 3⁵ˣ=81).

Base-exponent property: For any x,y, a>0, a≠1: aˣ=aʸ ⟺ x=y.

Steps:

  1. Isolate the exponential expression.
  2. Take the logarithm of both sides (use the power law to bring the exponent down).
  3. Solve for the variable.

Example: 2^(2x−1)=8=2³ → 2x−1=3 → x=2. (This is the x-coordinate where y=2^(2x−1) meets y=8.)

Example: 2^(x²−3x)=16=2⁴ → x²−3x=4 → x²−3x−4=0 → (x+1)(x−4)=0 → x=−1 or 4.

When bases differ: 2ˣ=20 → log2ˣ=log20 → x log2 = log20 → x=(log2+1)/log2 ≈ (0.3010+1)/0.3010 ≈ 4.322.

Solving 2ˣ=20 graphically

3.4.2 Solving Logarithmic Equations

A logarithmic equation involves the log of an expression with a variable (e.g., log₂(x+3)=4).

Steps:

  1. State the universe (the log's argument must be >0).
  2. Collect log terms on one side.
  3. Write in exponential form.
  4. Solve, then check the solution is in the universe.

Example: log₂(x+3)=4. Universe: x+3>0 → x>−3. x+3=2⁴=16 → x=13 (in universe). ✓

Example: log₃(5x−2)=2−log₃4. Universe x>2/5. log₃(4(5x−2))=2 → log₃(20x−8)=2 → 20x−8=9 → x=17/20 (>2/5 ✓).

Example: 3^(x+4)=2^(−x): (x+4)log3 = −x log2 → x(log3+log2) = −4log3 → x = −4log3/(log3+log2) ≈ −2.453.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Always state the universe (argument>0) before solving log equations, and verify the answer satisfies it. For exponential equations, use the base-exponent property when possible, else take logs.

3.5 Relation Between Exponential and Logarithmic Functions

y=aˣ and y=logₐx are inverses of each other (a>1, and the same holds for 0<a<1 with (½)ˣ and log(½)x).

Key relations:

  • Domain of aˣ = range of logₐx.
  • Range of aˣ = domain of logₐx.
  • x-axis is the horizontal asymptote of aˣ; y-axis is the vertical asymptote of logₐx.
  • (0,1) is the y-intercept of aˣ; (1,0) is the x-intercept of logₐx.
Family of logarithmic functions
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: The log function is the mirror image (reflection in y=x) of the exponential function with the same base. Domain/range and intercepts/asymptotes swap.

3.6 Applications

3.6.1 Compound Interest

Compound interest (Thm 3.5): A(t) = P(1 + r/n)^(nt)

where A(t)=amount after t years, P=principal, r=annual interest rate, n=compounds per year, t=years.

Continuously compounded: A(t) = Pe^(rt) (as n→∞).

Example: Birr 20,000 at 7% for 5 years:

  • annually: 20000(1.07)⁵ ≈ 28,051.03
  • semi-annually: 20000(1.035)¹⁰ ≈ 28,211.98
  • quarterly: 20000(1.0175)²⁰ ≈ 28,295.56
  • monthly: ≈ 28,352.51
  • daily: ≈ 28,380.40

More compounding → slightly higher amount.

Compound interest growth

3.6.2 Population Growth

P(t) = P₀e^(kt), k>0 (exponential growth), P₀ initial population, k growth rate.

Example: P₀=110 million, k=2.3%=0.023.

  • In 2018 (t=5): P(5)=110,000,000·e^(0.115) ≈ 123,406,078.
  • Doubling time: 2P₀ = P₀e^(0.023t) → e^(0.023t)=2 → 0.023t=ln2 → t=ln2/0.023 ≈ 30.14 years.

3.6.3 The pH Scale

pH = −log[H⁺] where [H⁺] is hydrogen-ion concentration in moles/liter.

  • pH=7 neutral; pH<7 acidic; pH>7 basic.

Example: Blood [H⁺]=4.53×10⁻⁸ → pH=−[log4.53 + log10⁻⁸]=−[0.6561−8]=7.344>7 → basic.

Example: Acid rain pH=2.4 → log[H⁺]=−2.4 → [H⁺]=antilog(−2.4)=3.98×10⁻³ M.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Compound interest A=P(1+r/n)^(nt) (→Pe^(rt) continuous); population P=P₀e^(kt); pH=−log[H⁺]. These are the three main application formulas.

📌 QUICK REVISION / MUST-KNOW BOX (Unit 3)

  • aᵐ·aⁿ=aᵐ⁺ⁿ; aᵐ/aⁿ=aᵐ⁻ⁿ; (aᵐ)ⁿ=aᵐⁿ; (ab)ⁿ=aⁿbⁿ; a⁰=1; a⁻ⁿ=1/aⁿ; a^(m/n)=(ⁿ√a)ᵐ.
  • logₐc=b ⟺ aᵇ=c; logₐ1=0; logₐa=1; logₐaᵖ=p; a^(logₐp)=p.
  • log(MN)=logM+logN; log(M/N)=logM−logN; logMʳ=r logM; change of base.
  • Common log=base10 (log); natural log=base e (ln); e≈2.718.
  • y=aˣ: domain ℝ, range (0,∞), y-int(0,1), asymp y=0; a>1 inc, 0<a<1 dec.
  • y=logₐx: domain (0,∞), range ℝ, x-int(1,0), asymp x=0; a>1 inc, 0<a<1 dec.
  • Log and exponential with same base are inverses (reflection in y=x).
  • Solve exponential: equal bases → equate exponents; else take logs.
  • Solve log: state universe, write exponential form, verify.
  • Compound: A=P(1+r/n)^(nt), continuous Pe^(rt); growth P₀e^(kt); pH=−log[H⁺].

UNIT 4: TRIGONOMETRIC FUNCTIONS

Note: Based on the official ANRSEB Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook (new curriculum, 2023), Unit 4.

4.1 Radian Measure of Angle

An angle is a measure of rotation of a ray about its vertex. The original ray is the initial side, the final position is the terminal side, and the rotation point is the vertex.

  • Anticlockwise rotation → positive angle. Clockwise → negative angle.

Standard position: vertex at origin, initial side along the positive x-axis.

Degree measure: one degree (1°) = 1/360 of a complete revolution. 1°=60′ (minutes), 1′=60″ (seconds).

Radian measure: an angle subtended by an arc equal in length to the radius has measure 1 radian. For an arc of length l in a circle of radius r subtending angle θ: θ = l/r or l = rθ.

Conversion: π rad = 180°.

  • Radians = (π/180)×degrees.
  • Degrees = (180/π)×radians.

Common conversions:

Degrees30456090180270360
Radiansπ/6π/4π/3π/2π3π/22π
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: π=180°. To convert deg→rad multiply by π/180; rad→deg multiply by 180/π. Arc length l=rθ (θ in radians).

Examples:

  • 120° = (π/180)·120 = 2π/3 rad.
  • (4/3)π = (180/π)·(4π/3) = 240°.
  • 6 rad = (180/π)·6 ≈ 343.6° (using π≈22/7).
  • Circle radius r, central angle 30° intercepts arc 11 cm: θ=π/6, r=l/θ=11/(π/6)=21 cm.
  • Minute hand 1.5 long, in 40 min turns (2/3)(360°)=(4π/3) rad → tip moves l=rθ=1.5·(4π/3)=2π units.

4.2 Basic Trigonometric Functions

For a right triangle with angle α:

  • sinα = opposite/hypotenuse = a/h
  • cosα = adjacent/hypotenuse = b/h
  • tanα = opposite/adjacent = a/b

For an angle θ in standard position with point P(x,y) on its terminal side and r=√(x²+y²):

  • sinθ = y/r, cosθ = x/r, tanθ = y/x.
  • cscθ = r/y, secθ = r/x, cotθ = x/y (reciprocals).

Example: P(5,12): r=√(25+144)=13 → sinθ=12/13, cosθ=5/13, tanθ=12/5.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: sin=opp/hyp, cos=adj/hyp, tan=opp/adj. In coordinate form, sin=y/r, cos=x/r, tan=y/x. r=√(x²+y²).

The unit circle

The unit circle has radius 1 centered at the origin. For a point P(a,b) on it with central angle x: cos x = a, sin x = b, so (a,b)=(cos x, sin x).

  • Since a²+b²=1: cos²x + sin²x = 1.
Unit circle with cosθ and sinθ

Quadrantal angles (multiples of π/2):

cos0=1,sin0=0; cos(π/2)=0,sin(π/2)=1; cosπ=−1,sinπ=0; cos(3π/2)=0,sin(3π/2)=−1; cos2π=1,sin2π=0.

  • Periodicity: sin(x+2πn)=sin x, cos(x+2πn)=cos x (n integer).
  • sin x=0 when x=nπ; cos x=0 when x=(2n+1)π/2.
  • sin(−x)=−sin x; cos(−x)=cos x; tan(−x)=−tan x.

Signs in quadrants (Table 4.3):

IIIIIIIV
sin++−−
cos+−−+
tan+−+−

Example: sin x>0 and cos x<0 → second quadrant.

Reciprocal functions: cscθ=1/sinθ, secθ=1/cosθ, cotθ=1/tanθ.

  • sec30°=1/cos30°=2/√3. sec60°+csc30°=2+2=4.
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Memorize the quadrant signs and the standard values. sin²x+cos²x=1 always. sin/cos are periodic with 2π.

4.2.2 Trigonometric values of angles

Complementary angles: sum to 90°. Complement of x is (90°−x).

  • sin(π/2−α)=cosα; cos(π/2−α)=sinα; tan(π/2−α)=cotα; cot(π/2−α)=tanα.

Example: sin54°=cos36°; if sin3A=cos(A−26°), then 90°−3A=A−26° → 4A=116° → A=29°.

Reference angle (θ_R): the positive acute angle between the terminal side and the x-axis.

  • QI: θ_R=θ; QII: θ_R=180°−θ; QIII: θ_R=θ−180°; QIV: θ_R=360°−θ.
  • The value of a trig function of θ equals ±the value at θ_R (sign by quadrant).

Example: θ=155° (QII): θ_R=25°, sin155°=sin25°, cos155°=−cos25°, tan155°=−tan25°.

Reference angle diagram

Supplementary angles: sum to 180°. sinθ=sin(180°−θ), cosθ=−cos(180°−θ), tanθ=−tan(180°−θ).

Co-terminal angles: share the same terminal side; differ by multiples of 360° (or 2π).

  • Degrees: θ±360n; radians: θ±2nπ.
  • Co-terminal angles have the same trig values.

Example: co-terminal of 30°: 390° (n=1), −690° (n=−2). Co-terminal of π/4: π/4−2π=−7π/4.

Example: sin780°: 780°=2×360°+60° → sin780°=sin60°=√3/2.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Reference angle: reduce to the acute angle with the x-axis; apply the sign from the quadrant. Co-terminal: add/subtract 360° (or 2π) any number of times.

Graphs of sine, cosine and tangent

Periodic function: repeats its values at regular intervals. The period is the repeating interval.

Sine y=sinθ: period 360° (2π), domain ℝ, range [−1,1]. Max 1 at π/2, min −1 at 3π/2.

Graph of y=sinθ

Cosine y=cosθ: period 360° (2π), domain ℝ, range [−1,1]. Max 1 at 0 and 2π, min −1 at π.

Graph of y=cosθ

Tangent y=tanθ: period 180° (π), domain {θ≠nπ/2, n odd}, range ℝ. Undefined at odd multiples of π/2 (vertical asymptotes).

Graph of y=tanθ
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: sin & cos: period 2π, range [−1,1]. tan: period π, range ℝ, undefined at odd multiples of π/2. Amplitude (for sin/cos) = max deviation from axis.

4.3 Trigonometric Identities and Equations

Pythagorean identities:

  1. sin²θ + cos²θ = 1
  2. 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ
  3. 1 + cot²θ = csc²θ

Example: θ in QIII, sinθ=−3/5 → cosθ=−√(1−9/25)=−4/5.

Example: θ in QIV, tanθ=−2 → sec²θ=1+4=5 → secθ=√5 (QIV cos>0), cosθ=1/√5.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: To find other trig ratios from one, use sin²+cos²=1 and the quadrant sign.

Addition/subtraction formulas:

  • sin(α+β)=sinαcosβ+cosαsinβ
  • sin(α−β)=sinαcosβ−cosαsinβ
  • cos(α+β)=cosαcosβ−sinαsinβ
  • cos(α−β)=cosαcosβ+sinαsinβ

Example: sin75°=sin(30°+45°)=sin30cos45+cos30sin45=(√2/2)(√3/2)+(√2/2)(1/2)=(√6+√2)/4. cos75°=(√6−√2)/4.

Double angle identities:

  • sin2θ=2sinθcosθ
  • cos2θ=cos²θ−sin²θ=1−2sin²θ=2cos²θ−1
  • tan2θ=2tanθ/(1−tan²θ)

Example: θ in QII, sinθ=3/5 → cosθ=−4/5 → sin2θ=2(3/5)(−4/5)=−24/25; cos2θ=cos²−sin²=7/25.

Half-angle identities:

  • sin(α/2)=±√((1−cosα)/2)
  • cos(α/2)=±√((1+cosα)/2)

(Sign depends on quadrant of α/2.)

Example: cos15°=cos(30°/2)=√((1+cos30°)/2)=√((1+√3/2)/2)=√(2+√3)/2.

Trigonometric equations

Solve using algebraic methods, identities, and reference angles. Use θ_R to find solutions in [0,2π), then add multiples of 2π.

Example: 2cosθ−1=0 → cosθ=1/2 → θ_R=π/3. cosθ>0 → QI & QIV → θ=π/3, 5π/3.

Example: 2sinθ=−1 → sinθ=−1/2 → θ_R=π/6. sin<0 → QIII & QIV → θ=7π/6, 11π/6 (then +2nπ).

Example: √3secθ+2=0 → cosθ=−√3/2 → θ_R=π/6. cos<0 → QII & QIII → θ=5π/6, 7π/6.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: For sinθ=k: use θ_R=sin⁻¹|k|; if k>0 solutions in QI&QII, if k<0 in QIII&QIV. For cosθ=k>0 in QI&QIV, k<0 in QII&QIII.

4.4 Applications of Trigonometric Functions

Angle of elevation: the angle the line of vision must be raised above the horizontal. Angle of depression: the angle it must be lowered below the horizontal.

Example: From a 40 m cliff, angle of depression 60° to an object at base level → tan60°=40/x → x=40/√3 m.

Example: 20 m rope, angle with ground 30° → sin30°=height/20 → height=10 m.

Example: Tree breaks; broken top touches ground 8 m from foot making 30° → tan30°=AB/8 → AB=8/√3, cos30°=8/AC → AC=16/√3; original height = AB+AC = 8√3 m.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: In right-triangle applications: identify the opposite/adjacent/hypotenuse relative to the given angle, then use sin, cos, or tan. Angles of elevation/depression are equal when lines are parallel (alternate angles).

📌 QUICK REVISION / MUST-KNOW BOX (Unit 4)

  • π rad = 180°; rad=deg×π/180; deg=rad×180/π; l=rθ.
  • sin=y/r, cos=x/r, tan=y/x; r=√(x²+y²).
  • csc=1/sin, sec=1/cos, cot=1/tan.
  • sin²+cos²=1; 1+tan²=sec²; 1+cot²=csc².
  • Reference angle θ_R by quadrant; co-terminal θ±360n/2πn.
  • Complementary: sinθ=cos(90°−θ); supplementary: sinθ=sin(180°−θ).
  • Addition/double/half-angle identities.
  • sin & cos: period 2π, range [−1,1]; tan: period π, range ℝ, undefined at odd π/2.
  • Solve trig equations using reference angle + quadrant signs + 2πn.
  • Angle of elevation/depression in right-triangle applications.

UNIT 5: CIRCLES

Note: Based on the official ANRSEB Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook (new curriculum, 2023), Unit 5.

5.1 Symmetrical Properties of Circles

Definition: A circle is the locus (set) of points in a plane equidistant from a fixed point (the center). The constant distance is the radius r.

  • Area: A = πr². Perimeter (circumference): P = 2πr.

Line of symmetry: a line about which the figure folds so one half coincides with the other. Any diameter of a circle is a line of symmetry; a circle has infinitely many lines of symmetry.

Example: A circle inscribed in a square has 4 lines of symmetry (those of the square).

Theorem 5.1: The line segment joining the center of a circle to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to the chord.

Chord with perpendicular from center

Theorem 5.2: The perpendicular drawn from the center of a circle to a chord bisects the chord.

Theorem 5.3: Equal chords of a circle are equidistant from the center.

Theorem 5.4: If the angles subtended by chords at the center are equal, the chords are equal.

Theorem 5.5: Equal chords subtend equal angles at the center.

Example: Chord of radius-5 cm circle is 8 cm long. Let M be midpoint: OM=√(OB²−MB²)=√(25−16)=√9=3 cm from center.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Center-to-midpoint-of-chord ⊥ chord; perpendicular from center bisects chord. Use the Pythagorean theorem (radius, half-chord, distance from center) for chord problems.

5.2 Angle Properties of Circles

  • Arc: a portion of the circumference. Major arc > 180° (3 letters); minor arc < 180° (2 letters).
  • Central angle: formed by two radii with vertex at the center.
  • Inscribed angle: vertex on the circle, formed by two chords.
Central vs inscribed angle

Theorem 5.6: If an inscribed angle and a central angle intercept the same arc, the inscribed angle is half the central angle (θ=2a).

Example: If central ∠POQ=150°, the inscribed angle PRQ (same arc) = 75°. Conversely, if ∠PRQ=75°, central ∠POQ=150°.

Theorem 5.7: Inscribed angles subtended by the same arc are equal.

Theorem 5.8 (Thales): An angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle (90°).

Angle in a semicircle = 90°

Example: AB is a diameter, ∠ACB=90° (Thales). In a triangle with another angle 55°, ∠BAC=35°.

Cyclic quadrilateral (Def 5.1): a quadrilateral whose four vertices lie on a circle.

Theorem 5.9: In a cyclic quadrilateral, the sum of either pair of opposite angles is 180°.

Cyclic quadrilateral with opposite angles summing to 180°

Example: A cyclic quadrilateral has angles (4y+2),(y+20),(5y−2),7y. Sum=360° → 17y+20=360 → y=20. So angles: 82°,40°,98°,140°.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Inscribed angle = ½ central angle (same arc). Inscribed angles on same arc are equal. Angle in a semicircle = 90°. Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°.

5.3 Arc Lengths, Perimeters and Areas of Segments and Sectors

Arc length (Def 5.2): s = 2πr·θ/360° (θ in degrees) [or s=πd·θ/360°].

Chord length: l = 2r·sin(θ/2), where θ is the central angle.

Example: Central angle 150° in circle radius 6 cm → arc length = 2π·6·(150/360) = 5π cm.

Example: θ=120°, r=8 → chord = 2·8·sin60° = 16·(√3/2) = 8√3 cm.

Segment (Def): the region bounded by a chord and an arc.

  • Perimeter of a segment = length of chord + length of arc.
Sector and segment of a circle

Sector (Def): the region bounded by two radii and an arc.

  • Area of a sector = πr²·θ/360°.
  • Perimeter of a sector = 2r + arc length = 2r + 2πr·θ/360°.

Example: sector radius 6 cm, angle 210° → Area=π·36·(210/360)=21π cm²; Perimeter=12+2π·6·(210/360)=12+7π cm.

Area of a segment = area of the sector − area of the triangle:

A = πr²·θ/360° − ½r²·sinθ.

Example: r=4, θ=60° → segment area = π·16·(1/6) − ½·16·sin60° = (8/3)π − 4√3.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: arc = 2πr·θ/360; sector area = πr²·θ/360; segment area = sector − triangle = πr²·θ/360 − ½r²sinθ. Chord = 2r·sin(θ/2).

5.4 Theorems on Angles and Arcs Determined by Lines Intersecting Inside, on and Outside a Circle

Theorem 5.10 (Chords intersecting inside): The measure of the angle formed between two intersecting chords equals ½ the sum of the intercepted arcs.

Two secants meeting outside a circle

Example: m(arcPQ)=68°, m(arcRS)=128°; chords PR and QS intersect at T → m∠RTS=½(68°+128°)=98°.

Theorem 5.11 (Secants & tangents intersecting outside): The angle formed by two secants, two tangents, or a secant and a tangent meeting outside the circle equals ½ the positive difference of the intercepted arcs.

  • Two secants: x=½[m(arcCE)−m(arcBD)].
  • Two tangents: x=½[m(arcBDC)−m(arcBC)].

Example: m(arcBD)=43°, m(arcCE)=107° → m∠CAE=½(107°−43°)=32°.

Additional facts:

  • Product of segments of intersecting chords: AP·PB = CP·PD.
  • Tangent line meets the circle at one point and is ⊥ to the radius to that point.
  • Tangents from an external point are equal in length.
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Chords inside → angle = ½(sum of arcs). Secants/tangents outside → angle = ½(difference of arcs). Tangent ⊥ radius at point of contact.

📌 QUICK REVISION / MUST-KNOW BOX (Unit 5)

  • Circle: A=πr², P=2πr; infinitely many lines of symmetry (any diameter).
  • Center–midpoint of chord ⊥ chord; perpendicular from center bisects chord.
  • Equal chords equidistant from center; equal chords subtend equal central angles.
  • Inscribed angle = ½ central angle (same arc); equal on same arc; 90° in semicircle.
  • Cyclic quadrilateral: opposite angles sum to 180°.
  • Arc s=2πr·θ/360; chord l=2r·sin(θ/2).
  • Sector area=πr²·θ/360; segment area=sector−triangle.
  • Chords inside: angle=½(sum arcs). Secants/tangents outside: angle=½(difference arcs).
  • Tangent ⊥ radius; equal tangents from external point.

UNIT 6: SOLID FIGURES

Note: Based on the official ANRSEB Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook (new curriculum, 2023), Unit 6.

6.1 Revision of Prisms and Cylinders

Right prism with base area BA, base perimeter p, altitude (height) h:

  • Lateral surface area LSA = p·h
  • Total surface area TSA = LSA + 2BA
  • Volume V = BA·h

Example (triangular prism): triangle sides 3,4,5 (right-angled, legs 3&4). p=3+4+5=12, h=6 → LSA=72 cm². BA=½·3·4=6 → TSA=72+12=84 cm². V=6·6=36 cm³.

Example (rectangular prism): 3×2 base, h=4 → LSA=40, BA=6, TSA=52, V=24.

Right circular cylinder with radius r, altitude h:

  • LSA = 2πrh
  • TSA = 2πrh + 2πr² = 2πr(h+r)
  • V = πr²h

Example: r=3, h=5 → TSA=2π·3·(5+3)=48π cm², V=π·9·5=45π cm³.

Example (hollow/annulus base): cylinder with inner radius 1, outer radius 4, h=6. BA=π(4²−1²)=15π; outer LSA=48π, inner LSA=12π → TSA=60π+2(15π)=90π; V=15π·6=90π.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: LSA = perimeter × height (prism) or 2πrh (cylinder). TSA adds two bases. V = base area × height for both.

6.2 Pyramids, Cones and Spheres

Pyramid (Def 6.1): a solid with a polygonal base and an apex (vertex) not in the base plane; each base point is joined to the apex.

  • Altitude/height: perpendicular from apex to the base plane.
  • Right pyramid: foot of altitude at the center of the base.
  • Regular pyramid: base is a regular polygon and lateral edges are equal.
Regular pyramid

Cone (Def 6.2): a pyramid whose base is a circular region. Right circular cone: foot of altitude at center of base.

  • Slant height l: the segment from the apex to a point on the base circle; l=√(h²+r²).
Right circular cone

Net (Def 6.3): a flat 2D pattern that folds into the 3D solid.

6.2.1 Surface Area of Pyramids and Cones

Regular pyramid (base perimeter p, slant height l, base area BA):

  • LSA = ½·p·l (½ × perimeter × slant height)
  • TSA = BA + ½pl

Example: regular square pyramid, base edge 4, slant height 5 → p=16, LSA=½·16·5=40, BA=16, TSA=56 cm².

Example: base edge 6, lateral edge 7 → slant height from half-base: l²=7²−3²=40 → l=2√10; LSA=½·24·2√10=24√10; BA=36; TSA=36+24√10.

Right circular cone (radius r, slant height l):

  • LSA = πrl (also = ½pl with p=2πr)
  • TSA = πrl + πr² = πr(l+r)
  • l = √(h²+r²)

Example: base diameter 8 (r=4), height 3 → l=√(9+16)=5 → LSA=20π, BA=16π, TSA=36π cm².

Cone with slant height
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Pyramid LSA = ½pl; cone LSA = πrl. Always find the slant height via l=√(h²+r²) for cones.

6.2.2 Horizontal cross-sections of pyramids and cones

Horizontal cross-section (Def 6.4): the intersection of the pyramid/cone with a plane parallel to the base plane.

Theorem 6.1: Every horizontal cross-section of a triangular pyramid is a triangle similar to the base.

Theorem 6.2/6.3: The ratio of the area of a cross-section to the area of the base is k²/h², where h is the altitude and k is the distance from the vertex to the cross-section plane.

Example: base area 270, h=6, cross-section 4 from vertex → A_cs/270=4²/6²=16/36 → A_cs=270·(4/9)=120 cm².

Example: square pyramid h=10, base side 5 → base area 25; cross-section 3 from vertex → A_cs/25=9/100 → A_cs=9/4 cm².

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Area ratio = (k/h)². When given distance from the base, k = h − (distance from base).

6.2.3 Volume of Pyramids and Cones

Cavalieri's Principle: two solids of equal height with equal cross-sectional areas at every level have equal volumes.

Theorem 6.7: Volume of a pyramid V = ⅓(BA)·h (base area × height ÷ 3).

Theorem 6.8: Volume of a cone V = ⅓πr²h.

Example: square pyramid base edge 4, h=7 → V=⅓·16·7=112/3 cm³.

Example: cone r=5, h=6 → V=⅓·π·25·6=50π cm³.

6.2.4 Surface Area and Volume of Sphere

Sphere (Def 6.5): a solid bounded by a closed surface every point of which is equidistant from a center.

  • Radius: segment from center to surface. Diameter: through the center to the surface.
  • Great circle: a cross-section through the center (radius = sphere's radius). Small circle: any other cross-section.
  • Hemisphere: one of the two halves divided by a great circle.
Sphere
  • Surface area: SA = 4πr²
  • Volume: V = 4/3πr³
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Sphere SA=4πr², V=4/3πr³. Pyramid/cone volume = ⅓(base area × height).

6.3 Frustum of Pyramids and Cones

Frustum of a pyramid (Def 6.6): the part of a pyramid between the base and a plane parallel to the base (the original base and the cross-section are the two bases; other faces are lateral faces, which are trapeziums).

Frustum of a cone (Def 6.7): the part of a cone between the base and a parallel plane.

Frustum of a cone

Frustum of a regular pyramid (lower perimeter p, upper p′, slant height l):

  • LSA = ½·l·(p + p′)

Example: square frustum, lower side 5, upper side 3, slant height 4 → p=20, p′=12 → LSA=½·4·(20+12)=64; TSA=64+5²+3²=98 cm².

Frustum of a right circular cone (radii r (bigger) and r′ (smaller), slant height l):

  • LSA = πl(r + r′)
  • TSA = πl(r+r′) + π(r²+r′²)

Volume of a frustum (cone or pyramid):

V = ⅓h(A + A′ + √(AA′)) (A, A′ base areas, h altitude)

For a cone: V = ⅓πh(r² + r′² + rr′).

Example: cone frustum height 24, base radius 22, slant height 26. l²=h²+(r−r′)² → 26²=24²+(22−r′)² → (22−r′)²=100 → r′=12. LSA=26π(22+12)=884π; TSA=884π+π(22²+12²)=884π+628π=1512π.

Example (volume): top & bottom diameters 6 & 10 (r′=3, r=5), h=12 → V=⅓π·12·(9+25+15)=196π≈615.44 m³.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Frustum LSA (cone)=πl(r+r′); volume=⅓πh(r²+r′²+rr′) or ⅓h(A+A′+√(AA′)). Find missing radius via l²=h²+(r−r′)².

6.4 Surface Area and Volume of Composed Solids

A composed solid is made of two or more solids. Volume = sum of the parts' volumes. Surface area = sum of exposed surfaces (be careful not to count hidden shared faces).

Composed solid (cylinder + cone)

Example (flask = frustum of cone + cylinder): frustum radii 4 & 8, slant height l=√(4²+16²)=4√17; cylinder radius 8, height 14.

  • TSA = frustum LSA (48√17π) + frustum lower base (64π) + cylinder LSA (2π·8·14=112π) = 16π(3√17+11).
  • Volume = frustum volume (⅓π·16·(64+16+32)=1792π/3) + cylinder volume (π·64·14=896π) = 4480π/3.

Example (cone + cylinder): cone radius 4 height 3 (l=5), cylinder radius 4 height 7.

  • TSA = cone LSA(20π) + cylinder LSA(56π) + cylinder lower base(16π) = 92π.
  • Volume = cylinder (π·16·7=112π) + cone (⅓π·16·3=16π) = 128π.

Example (drilled): cylinder radius 10, height 12, drilled a triangular prism (3-4-5 right triangle). TSA=2πrh+ph+2πr²−2(½ab)=240π+144+200π−12=(440π+132)≈1513.6. Volume=1200π−½·3·4·12=1200π−72≈3696.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Break into known solids, compute each, sum. For TSA count only exposed faces; for drilled/removed parts subtract.

6.5 Applications

Bucket (frustum of cone): bottom radius 10, top radius 13, slant height 20.

  • height h=√(20²−3²)=√391. Volume=⅓π·√391·(13²+10²+130)=⅓π·399√391≈8.26 liters (1 L=1000 cm³).
  • LSA=20π(13+10)=460π; plus bottom π(10²)=100π → TSA=560π≈1758.4 cm².
  • Cost at 50 Birr/100cm² = 1758.4·50/100 = 879.2 Birr.

Water tank (cylinder): hold 100,000 L=100 m³, height 8 m → πr²·8=100 → r≈2 m. Paint lateral surface (2cm thickness) → volume of paint = πh(R²−r²); painter cost = LSA × rate.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: 1 liter = 1000 cm³. Apply the frustum/cylinder formulas to real objects (bucket, tank, pipe, cone).

📌 QUICK REVISION / MUST-KNOW BOX (Unit 6)

  • Prism: LSA=ph, TSA=LSA+2BA, V=BA·h.
  • Cylinder: LSA=2πrh, TSA=2πr(h+r), V=πr²h.
  • Regular pyramid: LSA=½pl, TSA=BA+½pl, V=⅓(BA)h.
  • Cone: LSA=πrl, TSA=πr(l+r), V=⅓πr²h; l=√(h²+r²).
  • Sphere: SA=4πr², V=4/3πr³.
  • Cross-section area ratio = k²/h².
  • Frustum: cone LSA=πl(r+r′); volume=⅓πh(r²+r′²+rr′)=⅓h(A+A′+√(AA′)).
  • Composed solids: sum volumes; sum exposed areas.

UNIT 7: COORDINATE GEOMETRY

Note: Based on the official ANRSEB Grade 10 Mathematics Student Textbook (new curriculum, 2023), Unit 7.

7.1 Distance Between Two Points

The Cartesian (xy) plane is divided into four quadrants by the x-axis (horizontal) and y-axis (vertical), meeting at the origin (0,0). Each point is an ordered pair (x,y).

Distance formula (Def 7.1): For P(x₁,y₁) and Q(x₂,y₂),

d = √((x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²)

  • Horizontal: d=|x₂−x₁|. Vertical: d=|y₂−y₁|.
  • This follows from Pythagoras.
Distance between two points

Examples:

  • A(2,1), B(8,9): d=√(36+64)=10.
  • P(9,13), Q(4,1): d=√(25+144)=13.
  • R(0,−1), S(−3,3): d=√(9+16)=5.
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: d=√((Δx)²+(Δy)²). Distance is always positive (zero only if points coincide).

7.2 Division of a Line Segment

Section formula (internal, ratio p:q): The point R(x₀,y₀) dividing P(x₁,y₁)Q(x₂,y₂) internally in the ratio p:q is:

R = ( (p·x₂ + q·x₁)/(p+q) , (p·y₂ + q·y₁)/(p+q) )

Example: divide A(−7,4) and B(8,9) in ratio 3:2 (p=3,q=2): x=(3·8+2·(−7))/(3+2)=(24−14)/5=2; y=(3·9+2·4)/5=(27+8)/5=7 → R(2,7).

Midpoint formula: the midpoint M of P(x₁,y₁)Q(x₂,y₂) is

M = ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2)

Midpoint of a segment

Examples:

  • Midpoint of A(−1,−2), B(3,2) = ((−1+3)/2,(−2+2)/2)=(1,0).
  • If M(4,6) is the midpoint of AB and A=(−3,−2): (−3+x)/2=4 → x=11; (−2+y)/2=6 → y=14 → B(11,14).
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Section formula (p:q) uses (px₂+qx₁)/(p+q). Midpoint is the special case p:q=1:1 → averages of coordinates.

7.3 Equation of a Line

7.3.1 Gradient (slope)

Definition (Def 7.2): The gradient/slope m of a line through P(x₁,y₁), Q(x₂,y₂), x₁≠x₂:

m = (y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁) = (change in y)/(change in x)

  • Positive slope: line rises left→right. Negative: falls. Zero: horizontal. Vertical line: no slope (undefined).
Slope = rise over run

Examples:

  • P(2,1),Q(4,7): m=(7−1)/(4−2)=3.
  • P(7,3),Q(−4,3): m=0 (horizontal). P(2,3),Q(2,−7): undefined (vertical).

7.3.2 Slope in terms of angle of inclination

The inclination is the anticlockwise angle θ from the positive x-axis to the line (0°≤θ<180°).

m = tanθ

  • Acute inclination → positive slope; obtuse → negative slope (m=tan(180°−α)=−tanα).

Example: inclination 45° → m=tan45°=1. Inclination 120° → supplement 60° → m=−tan60°=−√3.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: slope = tan(inclination). Horizontal line has m=0; vertical line has no slope.

7.3.3 Different forms of the equation of a line

  • Point-slope form: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)
  • Slope-intercept form: y = mx + b (b = y-intercept)
  • Two-point form: y − y₁ = (y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁) · (x−x₁)
  • General form: Ax + By + C = 0
  • Intercept form: x/p + y/q = 1 (p=x-int, q=y-int)

Properties of m: m>0 line rises; m<0 line falls; m=0 horizontal; vertical line has no slope.

Examples:

  • m=3, b=−1 → y=3x−1.
  • m=4 through P(−5,0): y=4(x+5)=4x+20.
  • m=−2 through P(4,3): y−3=−2(x−4) → y=−2x+11.
  • Through (1,4),(2,6): m=2 → y−4=2(x−1) → y=2x+2.
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Use point-slope form with a given point & slope; slope-intercept for quick graphing; two-point form for two points. All can be written as Ax+By+C=0.

7.4 Parallel and Perpendicular Lines

Theorem 7.1 (Parallel): Two non-vertical lines are parallel iff they have the same slope (m₁=m₂).

Theorem 7.2 (Perpendicular): Two non-vertical lines are perpendicular iff m₁·m₂ = −1 (their slopes are negative reciprocals).

Parallel and perpendicular lines

Examples:

  • Line through P(6,4),R(7,11) has m=7; line through A(0,0),B(2,14) has m=7 → parallel.
  • Line through A(6,0),B(0,12) has m=−2; line through P(8,10),Q(4,8) has m=1/2 → −2·(1/2)=−1 → perpendicular.
  • Line through (5,4) parallel to y=2x+1 → y−4=2(x−5) → y=2x−6. Perpendicular → m=−1/2 → y=−½x+13/2.
✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Parallel ⟺ equal slopes. Perpendicular ⟺ slopes multiply to −1 (negative reciprocals).

7.5 Equation of a Circle

Definition (Def 7.2): A circle is the set of all points in a plane at a fixed distance (radius r) from a fixed point (center).

Standard form: (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r², center (h,k), radius r.

Center at origin: x² + y² = r².

Equation of a circle

General form (Def 7.3): x² + y² + lx + my + n = 0, with l²+m²−4n>0. Complete the square to find center/radius.

Examples:

  • Center (3,4), r=2 → (x−3)²+(y−4)²=4.
  • x²+y²−12x−16y+19=0 → (x−6)²+(y−8)²=81 → center (6,8), r=9.
  • Center (3,4) through P(5,6): r²=(5−3)²+(6−4)²=4+4=8 → (x−3)²+(y−4)²=8.

Special cases: l²+m²−4n=0 → point circle (radius 0); <0 → imaginary (no real circle).

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Circle equation needs center (h,k) and radius r. Complete the square to convert general form to standard form.

7.6 Applications

Area of a triangle with vertices (x₁,y₁),(x₂,y₂),(x₃,y₃):

A = ½|x₁(y₂−y₃) + x₂(y₃−y₁) + x₃(y₁−y₂)|

Example: A(−3,4),B(0,1),C(−3,−2): A=½|(−3)(1+2)+0(−2−4)+(−3)(4−1)|=½|−9+0−9|=9. AB=BC=3√2, slopes of AB and BC are −1 and 1 → product −1 → isosceles right-angled triangle.

Line equations of triangle sides & right-angle check: find the slope of each side, check if any two multiply to −1.

Example: Triangle A(−1,1),B(1,3),C(3,1): AB: y=x+2 (m=1); BC: y=−x+4 (m=−1); AC: y=1 (m=0). m₁·m₂=−1 → right-angled at B. BC's y-intercept is 4.

✍️ Must-know: ✍️ Must-know: Use the triangle area formula with absolute value. Use slopes to classify triangles (right if two slopes multiply to −1; isosceles if two sides equal).

📌 QUICK REVISION / MUST-KNOW BOX (Unit 7)

  • Distance: d=√((x₂−x₁)²+(y₂−y₁)²).
  • Section (p:q): R=((px₂+qx₁)/(p+q),(py₂+qy₁)/(p+q)).
  • Midpoint: ((x₁+x₂)/2,(y₁+y₂)/2).
  • Slope m=(y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁)=tanθ; horizontal m=0, vertical no slope.
  • Forms: point-slope y−y₁=m(x−x₁); slope-intercept y=mx+b; two-point; general Ax+By+C=0.
  • Parallel ⟺ m₁=m₂; perpendicular ⟺ m₁·m₂=−1.
  • Circle standard (x−h)²+(y−k)²=r²; origin x²+y²=r²; general x²+y²+lx+my+n=0.
  • Triangle area: ½|x₁(y₂−y₃)+x₂(y₃−y₁)+x₃(y₁−y₂)|.

📖 GLOSSARY OF KEY TERMS (quick definitions for revision)

Amplitude – the maximum deviation of a periodic function from its mean value (for sine/cosine, the height above/below the axis).

Angle of depression – the angle below the horizontal that an observer's line of vision is lowered to see an object.

Angle of elevation – the angle above the horizontal that an observer's line of vision is raised to see an object.

Angle of inclination – the anticlockwise angle from the positive x-axis to a line; its tangent equals the slope.

Antilogarithm – the number M such that log M = N; written antilog(N).

Apex – the vertex (top point) of a pyramid or cone not on the base.

Apothem – the perpendicular distance from the center of a regular polygon to a side.

Arc – a portion of the circumference of a circle (major > 180°, minor < 180°).

Arc length – the length of an arc, s = 2πr·θ/360°.

Asymptote – a line a graph approaches but never touches (x-axis for aˣ, y-axis for logₐx).

Axis of symmetry – the vertical line through the vertex of a parabola; also the line about which a figure is symmetric.

Base (of exponent) – the number being raised to a power in aⁿ.

Base (of logarithm) – the number a in logₐx.

Bijective (one-to-one correspondence) – a function that is both injective and surjective.

Central angle – an angle formed by two radii with vertex at the center of a circle.

Characteristic – the integer part of a common logarithm (the power of 10).

Chord – a line segment joining two points on a circle.

Circle – the locus of points in a plane equidistant from a fixed center.

Co-domain – the set of all possible outputs (B in f:A→B).

Co-terminal angles – angles in standard position that share the same terminal side (differ by multiples of 360° or 2π).

Common logarithm – logarithm to base 10, written log M.

Complementary angles – two angles whose sum is 90°.

Completing the square – rewriting ax²+bx+c as a(x+b/2a)² + (4ac−b²)/4a.

Cone – a pyramid with a circular base; right circular cone has its apex above the center.

Constant function – f(x)=b for all x; degree-0 polynomial (horizontal line).

Cyclic quadrilateral – a quadrilateral whose four vertices lie on a circle (opposite angles sum to 180°).

Degree (polynomial) – the highest exponent n of a polynomial.

Degree (angle) – 1/360 of a complete revolution.

Domain – the set of all inputs (x-values) for which a function is defined.

Exponent – the power to which a base is raised in aⁿ.

Exponential function – f(x)=aˣ, a>0, a≠1.

Factor theorem – f(c)=0 iff (x−c) is a factor of f(x).

Frustum – the part of a pyramid/cone between the base and a parallel cross-section.

Function – a relation in which no two distinct ordered pairs have the same first element.

Gradient (slope) – the ratio of vertical rise to horizontal run: m=(y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁).

Great circle – a cross-section of a sphere through its center (largest possible circle).

Hemisphere – one half of a sphere, divided by a great circle.

Inclination – see angle of inclination.

Injective (one-to-one) – each element of the domain maps to a distinct image.

Inscribed angle – an angle with vertex on the circle formed by two chords.

Inverse function – the function that reverses the mapping of f; y=logₐx is the inverse of y=aˣ.

Leading coefficient – the coefficient of the highest-degree term of a polynomial.

Linear function – f(x)=ax+b, a≠0; graph is a straight line.

Location theorem – if f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs, a zero lies between a and b.

Logarithm – the exponent to which a base must be raised to obtain a number: logₐc=b iff aᵇ=c.

Mantissa – the fractional part of a common logarithm.

Midpoint – the point halfway between two endpoints: ((x₁+x₂)/2,(y₁+y₂)/2).

Multiplicity (of a zero) – how many times a factor (x−c) appears in a polynomial.

Natural logarithm – logarithm to base e, written ln x.

One-to-one – see injective.

Onto (surjective) – every element of the co-domain has a pre-image.

Parabola – the U-shaped graph of a quadratic function.

Parallel lines – lines with the same slope (m₁=m₂).

Perpendicular lines – lines whose slopes multiply to −1 (m₁·m₂=−1).

Period – the interval after which a periodic function repeats (2π for sin/cos, π for tan).

Point-slope form – y−y₁=m(x−x₁).

Polynomial function – p(x)=aₙxⁿ+aₙ₋₁xⁿ⁻¹+…+a₀ with non-negative integer exponents.

Quadrantal angle – an angle that is an integral multiple of 90° (π/2).

Quadratic function – f(x)=ax²+bx+c, a≠0.

Radian – the angle subtended by an arc equal in length to the radius; π rad=180°.

Range – the set of all outputs of a function.

Rational Zero Test – method to find possible rational zeros p/q from factors of a₀ and aₙ.

Reciprocal functions – csc, sec, cot (reciprocals of sin, cos, tan).

Reference angle – the positive acute angle between the terminal side and the x-axis.

Relation – a set of ordered pairs.

Remainder theorem – the remainder of f(x)÷(x−c) is f(c).

Secant (geometry) – a line that intersects a circle at two points.

Sector – the region bounded by two radii and an arc.

Segment (circle) – the region bounded by a chord and an arc.

Slant height – the altitude of a lateral face of a pyramid/cone.

Slope-intercept form – y=mx+b.

Sphere – a solid bounded by a surface every point of which is equidistant from a center.

Supplementary angles – two angles whose sum is 180°.

Surjective – see onto.

Tangent (geometry) – a line that touches a circle at exactly one point.

Turning point (vertex) – the point where a graph changes direction.

Unit circle – a circle of radius 1 centered at the origin.

Vertex (parabola) – the turning point of a quadratic graph; the minimum or maximum.

Vertical line test – a graph is a function iff no vertical line cuts it more than once.

Zero of a function – a value c with f(c)=0 (a root of f(x)=0).
